name: Ragi Mudde
subtitle: smooth finger-millet balls, the everyday staple of the southern Karnataka plate

ingredients.note: fine, freshly milled if you can get it

prepNotes: Keep a bowl of cold water beside the stove — you shape the mudde with wet hands.
Mix 2 tbsp of the ragi flour into 1/2 cup cold water to a lump-free slurry before you start; this goes in first and stops the whole pot from seizing.
Have a heavy wooden spatula or a mudde kolu ready. A thin spoon will bend.

steps.text: Bring 4 cups water to a hard rolling boil with the salt in a heavy-bottomed pot.
Stir in the cold ragi slurry and let it boil 3 minutes until the water turns opaque brown and thickens slightly.
steps.tip: This pre-thickened base is what stops raw lumps forming later.

steps.text: Lower the heat to minimum and tip in the remaining ragi flour all at once, in a mound in the centre. Do not stir.
Cover and let it steam 5 minutes — the mound cooks through from the sides in.
steps.tip: Stirring now is the classic mistake. Let the steam do the work.

steps.text: Uncover and beat hard with the wooden spatula, pressing the dough against the side of the pot, for 4 to 5 minutes until it is one glossy, uniform mass with no pale flecks.
Cook another 3 minutes on low, folding the mass over itself, until it pulls cleanly away from the pot.
Wet your hands in the cold water, scoop out a fistful and roll it into a smooth ball the size of a small orange.
steps.tip: Work fast while it is hot; a cooled mass cracks instead of rounding.

steps.text: Serve immediately with hot saaru or bassaru, swallowing the pieces rather than chewing them.

storage: Best eaten within the hour. Leftover mudde stiffens; steam it for 5 minutes to soften, or crumble it into hot saaru.
